name: Makhuwa-Marrevone
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Kisseberth, Charles W. 2003 (Makhuwa P30 chapter, named on Glottolog makh1262 page)

new_statements.quote: Makhuwa is clearly a tonal language, but it has some intonational features as well. [...] In some Bantu languages, including some with a similar conjoint/disjoint distinction such as Makonde, Makwe, Zulu and Sotho, an automatic lengthening of the penultimate syllable occurs at the end of a phonological phrase, thus indicating the right boundary of that phrase. Unlike these languages, Makhuwa does not have this penultimate lengthening. [p. 34] — Makhuwa does not have automatic penultimate lenghtening as in other Bantu languages, such as Makwe and Makonde. [p. 20]

Locators check out: extracted text page 34 carries running head "20 Chapter 2." and line 27 reads "penultimate lenghtening as in other Bantu languages, such as Makwe and Makonde." new_statements.rule_in_words: Makhuwa (Enahara) is a tone language (mora-based H vs. toneless, with H doubling and final lowering); it has contrastive vowel length (o-mála 'to finish' vs o-máala 'to be quiet') and, unlike Makonde, Makwe, Zulu or Sotho, no automatic phrase-penultimate lengthening. The description gives no word-stress rule at all: stress is not mentioned in the phonology chapter.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the only length effects are lexical/derived long vowels and glide-triggered compensatory lengthening, not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: The statement concerns the phonological phrase (absence of the phrase-final penultimate lengthening that marks the right phrase edge in other Bantu languages); word-level stress is not discussed. Prosodic phrase edges are marked instead by tonal Final Lowering and by tone-doubling restrictions on the phrase-penult mora.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted description is of Makhuwa-Enahara (Ilha de Moçambique and the Nacala–Mogincual coast), which Glottolog 5.x classifies as the dialect Naharra (naha1263) under makh1262 (path maku1279 > makh1262 > naha1263), and which Ethnologue (19th ed., 2016) also lists under xmc ('Naharra (Enaharra)'), alongside Enlai, Makhuwana and Nampamela. It is NOT Emarevone proper (Moma/Mogincual/Pebane): Kröger 2005 (sec. 4.7) and the SIL 2010 vocabulary treat Enahara and Emarevoni as distinct varieties, and Kröger recommended Enahara, Empamela and Enlai be listed as dialects of central Makua with only Emarevone as 'Makua-Marevone'. Van der Wal (p. 2) explicitly extends her claims about 'Makhuwa' to other variants as probable. The Enlai (Angoche) tone data in Kisseberth 2003 and Kisseberth & Guérois 2014 belong to enla1242, which Glottolog places under makh1264 (vmw) although Ethnologue puts Enlai under xmc; those sources are silent on stress either way. No description of Emarevone proper (SIL 2010 vocabulary; Kröger 2005 survey) says anything about stress.

sources.note: Ch. 2 'A short description of Makhuwa-Enahara': p. 20 'Makhuwa does not have automatic penultimate lenghtening as in other Bantu languages, such as Makwe and Makonde' (contrastive length: o-mála 'finish' vs o-máala 'be quiet'); sec. 2.2 Prosody pp. 28-35 treats tone (mora = TBU, H doubling, final lowering); sec. 2.2.2 p. 34 'Makhuwa is clearly a tonal language... Unlike these languages, Makhuwa does not have this penultimate lengthening.' No word-stress statement. Variety = Enahara = Glottolog naha1263, a dialect of makh1262.

sources.citation: Ethnologue, 19th ed. (2016 web snapshot), entry xmc Makhuwa-Marrevone; Glottolog 5.3 pages makh1262, naha1263 (Naharra), enla1242 (Enlai), makh1264 (Makhuwa, vmw); SIL Language & Culture Archives listing for xmc (2015 snapshot); lidemo.net (SIL Moçambique) pages for xmc (2013 snapshots).
sources.note: Identity/inventory only: Ethnologue xmc dialects Makhuwana, Naharra (Enaharra), Enlai, Nampamela; Glottolog: Naharra naha1263 is a dialect of makh1262, Enlai enla1242 a dialect of makh1264 (vmw). SIL archive holds exactly two xmc items (the Emarevoni vocabulary and Kröger 2005). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Kisseberth, Charles W. & Rozenn Guérois. 2014. Melodic H tones in Emakhuwa and Ecuwabo verbs. Africana Linguistica 20: 181-205.
sources.note: Tone only; covers the 'coastal Nampula dialects Esaaka, Eeratti, and Enlai' (Enlai = 'a completely attenuating unrestricted doubling dialect, Nampula'); phrase-penult conditions on H doubling; no stress statement.

sources.citation: SIL Moçambique (Campos, Camulha, Daniel, Nabile, Rachide, Sunate; artist O. G. Nelly). 2009/2010. Vocabulário de Emakhuwa Emarevoni (Vocabulary of Emakhuwa Emarevoni). Línguas de Moçambique. Nampula: SIL Moçambique. 116 pp. (1st electronic ed. 2010; SIL archive 42918).
sources.note: Only an alphabet table ('O Alfabeto': vowels a e i o u and long aa ee ii oo uu with examples; consonants) plus a ~1,700-word Portuguese-Emarevoni list; nothing on tone, accent or stress. Locates Emarevoni in part of Moma, Mogincual and part of Pebane, separate from Enahara (Mossuril, Ilha de Moçambique, Nacala, Memba).

sources.citation: Kröger, Oliver. 2005. Report on a survey of coastal Makua dialects. SIL Electronic Survey Reports 2005-020. Dallas: SIL International. 45 pp.
sources.note: Sociolinguistic survey (lexicostatistics, RTT, interviews) of Enahara, Enlai/Empamela, Emarevone (Moma district; 65% apparent cognates with central Makua) and Emoniga. Tone appears only in passing (sec. 4.6: orthography details 'like word boundaries... or tone'; sec. 4.8: 'Tonal variation has been described at length by Cassimijee and Kisseberth (1999)'). No stress or accent statement. Sec. 4.7 recommends Emarevone as the separate Ethnologue entry 'Makua-Marevone' and Enahara, Empamela, Enlai as dialects of (central) Makua.

sources.citation: Kisseberth, Charles W. 2003. Makhuwa (P30). In Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 546-565. London: Routledge.
sources.note: The source the earlier scan named. Sec. 3 Phonology (vowels, consonants, syllable structure with contrastive long vowels, sec. 3.4 Tone pp. 553-555) is tone-only; Enlai (Angoche) is described as a doubling dialect with primary H fully low, doubling into phrase-final position and onto the second mora of a bimoraic phrase-penult syllable. No mention of stress, accent or penultimate lengthening anywhere in the chapter. Data dialects are Ikorovere/Imitthupi (Tanzania); Enahara and Enlai only named/compared.

sources.citation: Cassimjee, Farida & Charles W. Kisseberth. 1999. A conspiracy argument for Optimality Theory: Emakhuwa dialectology. University of Pennsylvania Working Papers in Linguistics 6(1): 81-96.
sources.note: Tone (Ikorovere, Eerati, Esaaka); no coastal Marrevone/Enlai/Enahara data; no stress statement (grep).
